steps.say: Ultrasound sees inflammation before the exam does. Power Doppler indicates sites where new vessels feed the pannus. That signal indicates ongoing damage and requires treatment escalation. This figure indicates how sacroiliac and spinal inflammation appear on imaging.
steps.tx: Musculoskeletal ultrasound (**MSUS**, sound wave imaging of joints) detects subclinical synovitis (silent joint lining inflammation) and tenosynovitis (tendon sheath inflammation) with high sensitivity. **Power Doppler** signal indicates active hypervascular synovial proliferation and correlates with ongoing structural damage in rheumatoid arthritis (a chronic erosive joint disease). A Doppler positive joint requires treat to target intensification even when the examination feels quiet.

vis.alt: Two panel illustration of axial spondyloarthritis imaging showing sacroiliac inflammation and progressive spinal ankylosis.
vis.caption: Imaging reveals sacroiliitis long before plain films change. Doppler and MRI activity both require escalation, not watching. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: The double contour sign is gout seen on ultrasound. A bright band is present over the cartilage surface. Its specificity is above 90 percent. Cartilage calcification instead indicates CPPD, so the two findings point in opposite directions.
steps.tx: The ultrasound **double contour sign** (a bright second line over cartilage) is a hyperechoic irregular band over the superficial surface of hyaline cartilage (smooth joint cartilage). It carries above **90 percent** specificity for monosodium urate (gout crystal) deposition, distinct from cartilage calcification which indicates calcium pyrophosphate disease instead. When the band is present over cartilage like icing, gout is the working diagnosis until proven otherwise.

steps.say: MRI with STIR sequences indicates bone marrow edema at the sacroiliac joints. That edema is required for the imaging arm of the ASAS criteria. Plain films are normal for years, so a normal X-ray never excludes early disease.
steps.tx: In spondyloarthritis (inflammatory spine and sacroiliac disease), MRI of sacroiliac joints with short tau inversion recovery (**STIR**, a fluid sensitive sequence) or T2 fat suppressed views identifies active sacroiliitis through periarticular **bone marrow edema** (inflammatory fluid in subchondral bone). This edema is mandatory for the imaging arm of ASAS axial SpA criteria. Radiographs lag symptoms by years, so MRI is required whenever inflammatory back pain meets a normal X-ray.

steps.say: Dual energy CT is the test that colour codes urate deposits using two X-ray energies. Sensitivity and specificity are above 85 percent. It is most useful where gout hides, such as the spine or an odd joint. The knee film here is the plain film counterpart in CPPD.
steps.tx: Dual energy computed tomography (**DECT**, two energy X-ray scanning) exploits attenuation differences at **80 kVp and 140 kVp** to colour code monosodium urate deposits, with sensitivity and specificity above **85 to 90 percent**. It proves invaluable for atypical tophaceous gout (spine, finger pads, or prosthetic joints). The knee radiograph shows the counterpart finding in CPPD: meniscal **chondrocalcinosis** (fibrocartilage calcification) marked by arrows, not urate.

vis.alt: Knee radiograph with arrows marking meniscal chondrocalcinosis and joint space narrowing in CPPD.
vis.caption: Arrows mark meniscal calcification of chondrocalcinosis. DECT instead colour codes urate in gout. Image: Taokinesis, annotated by Mikael Haggstrom.

steps.say: Early rheumatoid films indicate soft swelling and thin bone around the joint. Erosions then involve the bare areas of the knuckles. The second and third MCP joints are the classic sites. Both hands require comparison against this sequence at every visit.
steps.tx: Conventional radiography in early rheumatoid arthritis shows periarticular **osteopenia** (thin bone around the joint) and soft tissue swelling, progressing to marginal cortical **erosions** (bites at the edge) at bare areas (synovial reflection without cartilage) of the second and third metacarpophalangeal (**MCP**, knuckle) and third proximal interphalangeal joints. Erosions at these bare areas are the radiographic signature that separates rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis.

steps.say: Thin vertical bridges between vertebrae are the mark of ankylosing spondylitis. Thick horizontal flowing bone indicates DISH. The bamboo spine develops only after years of syndesmophytes. Squaring and shiny corners are the earlier clues to catch.
steps.tx: In ankylosing spondylitis (progressive spinal fusion disease), spinal films reveal vertebral body **squaring** (lost anterior concavity), Romanus lesions (erosive shiny corners), and thin delicate vertical **syndesmophytes** (bony bridges from the annulus fibrosus) producing bamboo spine. Thick coarse flowing horizontal osteophytes instead indicate diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (**DISH**, degenerative stiffening disease). Vertical delicate bridges require a spondylitis label, while horizontal flowing bone does not.

steps.say: PET-CT indicates inflamed large arteries before they narrow. Uptake brighter than the liver indicates active vasculitis in Takayasu and giant cell arteritis. It is a survey of the whole aorta in one sitting. Biopsy is still the decider in cranial disease.
steps.tx: Glucose analogue PET scanning with CT (**FDG PET-CT**, metabolic imaging of inflammation) detects large artery vasculitis in Takayasu disease (pulseless illness of young women) and giant cell arteritis. A continuous ring of tracer around the **aorta** (the central great artery) and its main branches, brighter than liver, indicates active wall inflammation before any narrowing develops. One whole body acquisition maps every territory at once, while cranial disease still requires temporal artery biopsy.

rows: Whole aorta survey in large vessel vasculitis

steps.say: Nailfold capillaroscopy is the test that separates primary Raynaud from scleroderma. Giant loops above 50 micrometers with dropout indicate the scleroderma pattern. A normal bed points to primary Raynaud. Every Raynaud patient requires one look at the nailfold.
steps.tx: Nailfold capillaroscopy (200x microscopic nail bed viewing) detects microvascular architecture. The **scleroderma pattern** features giant capillary loops (diameter above **50 micrometers**), microhaemorrhages, avascular areas, and neoangiogenic arborization (bushy new vessels), distinguishing primary Raynaud (benign cold induced spasm) from systemic sclerosis. A giant loop with dropout indicates secondary disease and requires autoantibody testing, while a normal bed reassures.
